subject: Connectivity decision: endpoint vs peering vs encrypted tunnel for EdgeCorp private deployment
messages:
From: Raj Patel <raj.patel@edgecorp.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
Cc: ops@edgecorp.com
Date: Tue, 30 May 2028 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Connectivity options for EdgeCorp private deployment

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the call this morning. We're moving forward with a private deployment of Redwood in our us-west-2 region and need a short recommendation on the connectivity approach. High level constraints:
- Sensitive PII workloads, so traffic must not traverse the public internet where avoidable.
- Peak throughput ~3.5 Gbps sustained, spiky bursts to 6 Gbps.
- Prefer to preserve client source IPs for existing auth/ACLs.
- Want a low ops-maintenance option but need a tested DR/failover path.

We're trying to choose between: VPC peering (same-account and cross-account), AWS PrivateLink/interface endpoints, or an IPsec site-to-site VPN (BGP) as primary. Can you sketch the tradeoffs (latency, cost, failover, NAT/hairpin issues, operational overhead) and a recommended default pattern?

Attached: current VPC topology and expected CIDR ranges.

Appreciate a short write-up we can take to our networking team.

-Raj

[Attachment: edgecorp-vpc-topology.v1.pdf (topology diagram)]

From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
To: Raj Patel <raj.patel@edgecorp.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 30 May 2028 11:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Connectivity options for EdgeCorp private deployment

On Tue, May 30, 2028 at 9:12 AM Raj Patel <raj.patel@edgecorp.com> wrote:
> Thanks again for the call this morning...

Raj — thanks for the clear constraints. Below is a concise comparison and a recommended hybrid pattern that balances your throughput, security, and ops goals. I'm keeping the summary non-cloud-vendor-specific where possible but will call out AWS specifics since your topology is in us-west-2.

Short summary (TL;DR):
- If you have both accounts in the same AWS Organization and cross-account peering is feasible, VPC peering (or Transit Gateway) gives simplest, lowest-latency path for high-throughput internal traffic, preserves source IPs, and has predictable costs (data transfer + possible TGW fees).
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is great for tight security/perimeter control and avoids hairpinning for cross-account service exposure; however it introduces additional ENI/endpoint costs, per-GB charges for endpoint data processing, and does not natively support 6+ Gbps from a single endpoint without multiple endpoints/load balancers. Also source IP preservation requires proxying; outgoing source IPs will typically be the endpoint ENI.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec with BGP) provides cross-region/account connectivity and is simple to set up as a backup or for on-prem integration, but adds higher latency, potential MTU fragmentation, and variable throughput depending on vendor. Managed VPN (AWS VPN / partner VPN) can be used for failover.

Key tradeoffs (expanded):
- Latency: Peering/TGW < PrivateLink (slight overhead) < IPsec VPN. Expect <1ms for same-AZ peering, ~1-3ms for cross-AZ/region peering/TGW, +1-5ms for PrivateLink depending on NLB/proxy path, VPN adds 10s of ms in many cases.
- Throughput: Peering/TGW handles multi-Gbps easily. PrivateLink depends on the NLB / ENI scaling—plan for horizontal endpoints and LB. VPN throughput often limited by tunnel endpoints and CPU crypto limits; managed IPSec can reach multi-Gbps with HA pairs but is more operationally heavy.
- Source IP: Peering preserves client source IPs. PrivateLink typically masks source IP (unless you run passthrough proxies and inject X-Forwarded-For). VPN preserves source if routed correctly but may require NAT to avoid overlapping CIDRs.
- Hairpinning & asymmetry: PrivateLink can cause hairpin routes when clients and service are in same VPCs or peering; peering avoids hairpins if route tables are correct. Watch for asymmetric routing with multiple tunnels/load paths—BGP route priorities matter.
- Security & audit: PrivateLink reduces attack surface (no public IPs on endpoints) and is easiest to reason about for compliance reviewers. Peering/TGW requires strict route table and SG controls; with peering, you must ensure VPC firewall rules prevent accidental broad exposure.
- Cost: Peering charges cross-AZ/region transfer; PrivateLink has per-hour endpoint and per-GB processing fees; TGW has attachment/hour fees and inter-region data costs. VPN has lower steady fees but can be costlier at high egress. We'll draft a small cost example if you want.

Recommended approach for EdgeCorp (given constraints):
1) Primary: Transit Gateway-based peering fabric (or direct VPC peering if you prefer smaller scale) for the data plane
   - Rationale: preserves source IP, scales to multi-Gbps without per-endpoint engineering, predictable latency.
   - Operational notes: attach Redwood subnets to the TGW, use route table separation by environment (prod/non-prod), and enforce SGs and least-privilege routes.
2) PrivateLink for control plane and sensitive management interfaces
   - Rationale: expose only the minimal set of management APIs (admin, audit, metrics) via interface endpoints to limit surface area and simplify compliance review.
   - Operational notes: provision multiple endpoints across AZs and put an internal NLB in front of your Redwood service to distribute. Accept that the source IP will be the ENI; use X-Forwarded-For or mutual TLS for auth.
3) IPsec S2S VPN as DR/backup and for on-prem interconnect
   - Rationale: low-touch fallback path when TGW/peering goes down or for on-prem sites. Configure BGP with disjoint ASNs and set appropriate MED/LOCAL_PREF for failover.

Mutual action plan (MAP)
- Week 0: Finalize CIDR overlap check (EdgeCorp infra) and decide TGW vs direct peering. (owner: EdgeCorp networking)
- Week 1: Redwood provides Terraform module for TGW + route tables + SG templates. (owner: Soojin)
- Week 2: Provision PrivateLink endpoints for control plane and run compliance scan. (owner: Redwood infra + EdgeCorp security)
- Week 3: Test S2S VPN with BGP failover, validate throughput and MTU. (owner: EdgeCorp ops)

Attachments: I attached a quick diagram and a cost sketch (see attached XLSX).

If you want, Connor can run a short perf test with a 6-minute sustained throughput run to show expected latency and packet-loss for TGW vs a VPN tunnel.

Thanks — will follow up with a one-page architecture sketch.

--
Soojin Lee
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
soojin_lee@redwood.ai

Soojin — really helpful, thank you. A couple quick clarifying questions from our network team:
1) We have overlapping legacy on-prem ranges in 10.0.0.0/8 that we can't renumber quickly. Will TGW/peering force us to renumber?
2) For PrivateLink, you mentioned source IP masking — we need client IPs for our WAF-based rules. Is that solvable without full proxying?

Also, can you include expected monthly cost ballpark for 3.5TB/month egress and 6 Gbps bursts under the TGW vs PrivateLink vs VPN options?

-Raj

[EdgeOps: please see Q1/2 below]

From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
To: Raj Patel <raj.patel@edgecorp.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.ai>, Samir Khanna <samir@consultancy.ai>
Date: Fri, 02 Jun 2028 10:15:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Connectivity options for EdgeCorp private deployment

Raj — quick answers below, with recommended mitigations: 

1) Overlapping on-prem CIDR:
- TGW/peering does not force renumbering but overlapping CIDRs must be avoided for direct routing. Options:
  a) Use NAT translation (SNAT/DNAT) at the on-prem egress to present non-overlapping CIDRs to the cloud (operationally heavier).
  b) Put the Redwood workload in a dedicated, non-overlapping VPC and use Proxy/NAT at the boundary; route specific prefixes via VPN with NAT.
  c) Use PrivateLink for the management/control plane so your on-prem clients can reach services without route propagation; for data plane, NAT at edge might be simplest short-term.

Recommendation: Given the renumbering cost, plan for short-term NATing for the on-prem->cloud flows and a medium-term CIDR carveout project so peering/TGW can be cleaner.

2) PrivateLink & client IPs:
- The interface endpoint model will place an ENI in your VPC; by default the service will see the ENI private IP as the source. To retain client IPs without heavy proxying you can:
  a) Use an internal NLB in front of the Redwood service with the NLB preserving the client source IP when used together with target type IP (requires careful health-check setup).
  b) Use X-Forwarded-For (application layer) and ensure your WAF/policies can parse it (less ideal for rule enforcement at L3/L4).
  c) Run a small NAT gateway that injects a unique source range per client subnet and map back in logs (operational).

Practical note: if preserving true client source IP at L3 is a hard requirement, TGW/peering is the cleanest. PrivateLink is better for tighter control and compliance but needs some application changes for IP visibility.

3) Ballpark cost (monthly, rough) for 3.5 TB/month egress and expected burst profile:
- TGW/Peering: data transfer charges apply per-GB (region-internal cheaper). Estimate: $400–$1,200/month depending on cross-AZ/region traffic patterns + small Transit Gateway attachment fees.
- PrivateLink: endpoint hourly + per-GB processing + NLB charges; estimate $1,200–$2,200/month if you need multi-AZ, with higher ops for scaling endpoints during bursts.
- VPN (managed): lower base cost but likely higher per-GB egress and ops; estimate $600–$1,500/month but throughput and reliability vary.

I'll pull a spreadsheet with a few scenarios and drop it into the shared link.

--
Soojin

Raj / Soojin — I ran a quick perf sanity test in a mirror environment for TGW vs an IPSec tunnel at sustained 6-minute intervals: TGW showed stable <2ms added latency and negligible jitter at 5 Gbps; IPSec tunnel averaged +18ms and occasional MTU fragmentation at 6 Gbps when encryption CPU spiked.
